topics.title: Structure & Bonding
topics.concept:
Organic chemistry is the study of carbon compounds, and almost everything about how a molecule behaves follows from how its atoms are connected. Carbon has four valence electrons and completes its octet by forming four bonds. A Lewis structure shows this sharing: lines are bonding pairs and dots are lone pairs. You can check a structure's charge with formal charge = (valence electrons) − (lone-pair electrons) − ½(bonding electrons).

Hybridization explains molecular shape. When carbon forms four single bonds, it uses four equivalent sp³ orbitals arranged tetrahedrally, with bond angles of 109.5° (methane, CH₄). A carbon with a double bond is sp² hybridized: three orbitals lie in a plane 120° apart (trigonal planar) and one unhybridized p orbital forms the π bond (ethene, C₂H₄). A carbon with a triple bond is sp hybridized and linear at 180° (ethyne, C₂H₂). Lone pairs also matter: nitrogen in ammonia (NH₃) is sp³ with a ~107° angle, and oxygen in water (H₂O) is sp³ with a ~104.5° angle, because lone pairs occupy more space and squeeze the bonds together.

Bond polarity comes from electronegativity — an atom's pull on shared electrons. On the Pauling scale, the key values are F 4.0, O 3.5, N 3.0, Cl 3.2, C 2.5, and H 2.2. A bond between atoms of different electronegativity is polar covalent: the more electronegative atom carries a partial negative charge (δ−) and the other a partial positive charge (δ+). The size of the difference tells you how polar the bond is, which in turn helps predict reactivity and whether a molecule has a net dipole moment.

questions.prompt: What is the hybridization of the carbon atom in methane (CH₄)?
questions.explanation: Methane's carbon forms four single bonds, so it has four electron groups. Four groups = sp³ hybridization, which gives a tetrahedral geometry.

questions.prompt: What is the approximate H–C–H bond angle around a tetrahedral (sp³) carbon?
questions.explanation: Tetrahedral geometry places the four bonds as far apart as possible, giving 109.5° bond angles.

questions.prompt: Each carbon in ethene (C₂H₄) is sp² hybridized. What shape does this produce around each carbon?
questions.explanation: sp² gives three orbitals in a plane 120° apart (trigonal planar). The remaining unhybridized p orbital forms the π bond of the C=C double bond.

questions.prompt: Which element has the highest electronegativity on the Pauling scale?
questions.explanation: Fluorine is the most electronegative element (about 4.0). The order is F > O (3.5) > N (3.0) > C (2.5).

questions.prompt: What is the hybridization of each carbon atom in ethyne (HC≡CH)?
questions.explanation: Ethyne has a C≡C triple bond. Each carbon has two electron groups (one σ bond to the other carbon and one to hydrogen), so it is sp hybridized and linear at 180°.

questions.prompt: How many valence electrons does a neutral carbon atom have?
questions.explanation: Carbon is in group 14, so it has four valence electrons and forms four bonds to complete its octet.

questions.prompt: What is the formal charge on the nitrogen atom in NH₄⁺ (ammonium)?
questions.explanation: Formal charge = valence − (lone-pair electrons) − ½(bonding electrons). Nitrogen has 5 valence electrons, 0 lone pairs, and 4 bonds (8 bonding electrons, half = 4): 5 − 0 − 4 = +1.

questions.prompt: Which of these bonds is the most polar?
questions.explanation: Polarity follows the electronegativity difference. O–H (3.5 − 2.2 = 1.3) is larger than C–Cl (3.2 − 2.5 = 0.7), C–H (0.3), and C–C (0).

topics.title: Nomenclature
topics.concept:
IUPAC nomenclature is a systematic way to name organic molecules so that each name describes an unambiguous structure. To name an alkane, you find the longest continuous carbon chain (the parent), number it so that substituents get the lowest possible numbers, then name each substituent as a prefix and the chain as a suffix.

The root gives the number of carbons in the parent chain: meth- (1), eth- (2), prop- (3), but- (4), pent- (5), hex- (6), hept- (7), oct- (8), non- (9), dec- (10). The suffix gives the family: -ane for alkanes (all single bonds), -ene for alkenes (a C=C double bond), -yne for alkynes (a C≡C triple bond), -ol for alcohols, -al for aldehydes, -one for ketones, and -oic acid for carboxylic acids.

Substituents are named from their own carbon count with the ending -yl (methyl = CH₃–, ethyl = CH₃CH₂–, propyl = CH₃CH₂CH₂–). When a substituent appears more than once, use the prefixes di- (2), tri- (3), tetra- (4). Numbers (locants) tell you where each substituent or functional group sits on the chain, and substituent names are listed in alphabetical order (ignoring di-/tri- prefixes).

For example, CH₃CH₂CH₃ is propane (three carbons, saturated). CH₃CH₂OH is ethanol (two carbons plus an –OH). CH₃CH=CH₂ is propene. The branched molecule (CH₃)₂CHCH₃ has a three-carbon parent (propane) with a methyl on carbon 2, so it is 2-methylpropane.

resources.title: IUPAC (International Union of Pure and Applied Chemistry)

questions.prompt: What is the IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: The longest chain has three carbons, so the root is 'prop-'. It has only single bonds, so the suffix is '-ane': propane.

questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms are in the parent chain of 2-methylpentane?
questions.explanation: The root 'pent-' means five carbons. The '2-methyl' is a one-carbon substituent attached to carbon 2 of that five-carbon chain.

questions.prompt: Give the IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂OH.
questions.explanation: A two-carbon chain (eth-) with an –OH group (alcohol) gives the suffix '-ol': ethanol.

questions.prompt: What does the suffix '-ene' indicate?
questions.explanation: '-ene' indicates a carbon–carbon double bond (an alkene). '-ane' = alkane, '-ol' = alcohol, '-oic acid' = carboxylic acid.

questions.prompt: What is the IUPAC name for CH₃CH₂CH₂CH₃?
questions.explanation: Four carbons in a continuous chain give the root 'but-', and all single bonds give '-ane': butane.

questions.prompt: Give the IUPAC name for CH₃CH=CH₂ (a three-carbon chain with a double bond).
questions.explanation: Three carbons (prop-) plus a C=C double bond (-ene): propene. The double bond position is unambiguous here, so no locant is required.

questions.prompt: How many carbon atoms total are in 2,3-dimethylbutane?
questions.explanation: The 'butane' parent has four carbons, plus two methyl substituents (one carbon each) = six carbons total (C₆H₁₄).

questions.prompt: Which root indicates a seven-carbon chain?
questions.explanation: hept- = 7 carbons (hex- = 6, oct- = 8, non- = 9).

topics.title: Functional Groups
topics.concept:
A functional group is a specific atom or group of atoms that gives a molecule its characteristic chemical reactions. Recognizing these groups is the single most important skill in organic chemistry, because molecules are classified and named by them.

The most common groups to know: an alcohol has an –OH group bonded to carbon (R–OH). A carboxylic acid has a –COOH group — a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to an –OH (R–COOH). An amine contains nitrogen bonded to carbon and/or hydrogen (R–NH₂, R₂NH, or R₃N). A ketone has a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to two carbons (R–CO–R′), while an aldehyde has the carbonyl bonded to at least one hydrogen (R–CHO). An ester has R–COO–R′ (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is also bonded to carbon), and an amide has R–CO–NR₂ (a carbonyl bonded to a nitrogen). An ether is simply an oxygen bonded to two carbons (R–O–R′), and an alkyl halide has a halogen bonded to carbon (R–X).

The difference between an aldehyde and a ketone is easy to miss: in an aldehyde the carbonyl carbon is bonded to one hydrogen and one carbon; in a ketone it is bonded to two carbons. That single hydrogen changes the naming (suffix -al vs -one) and the chemistry. Similarly, the difference between an ester and an ether is that an ester always contains a carbonyl, while an ether does not.

questions.prompt: Which functional group does CH₃COOH contain?
questions.explanation: The –COOH group is a carboxylic acid: a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to an –OH group.

questions.prompt: What is the key structural difference between an aldehyde and a ketone?
options: Aldehydes contain nitrogen; ketones do not
The carbonyl carbon in an aldehyde is bonded to at least one hydrogen; in a ketone it is bonded to two carbons
questions.explanation: In an aldehyde (R–CHO), the carbonyl carbon is bonded to a hydrogen and one carbon. In a ketone (R–CO–R′), it is bonded to two carbons.

questions.prompt: Name the functional group in CH₃OH.
questions.explanation: CH₃OH has an –OH group bonded to a carbon, which is the alcohol functional group (methanol).

questions.prompt: Which of these is an amine?
questions.explanation: CH₃NH₂ contains nitrogen bonded to carbon and hydrogen — an amine. The others are an alcohol, a carboxylic acid, and a ketone.

questions.prompt: What functional group is present in CH₃COCH₃ (acetone)?
questions.explanation: Acetone has a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to two carbon atoms (one on each side), which is a ketone.

questions.prompt: Name the functional group in CH₃OCH₃.
questions.explanation: An oxygen bonded to two carbon atoms (R–O–R′) is an ether. CH₃OCH₃ is dimethyl ether.

questions.prompt: Which structure contains an ester group?
questions.explanation: An ester has the form R–COO–R′ (a carbonyl bonded to an oxygen that is also bonded to carbon). CH₃COOCH₃ (methyl acetate) is an ester; the others are an alcohol, a ketone, and an amine.

questions.prompt: An amide group contains a carbonyl (C=O) bonded to…
questions.explanation: An amide has R–CO–NR₂: a carbonyl carbon bonded to a nitrogen atom (for example, acetamide CH₃CONH₂).

topics.title: Stereochemistry
topics.concept:
Stereochemistry is the study of how molecules are arranged in three-dimensional space. Two molecules can have the same atoms connected in the same order yet still be different, because those atoms point in different directions in space.

A carbon atom bonded to four different groups is called a chiral center (or stereocenter). A molecule with a chiral center is chiral: it is not superimposable on its mirror image, just like your left and right hands. The two mirror-image forms are enantiomers. Enantiomers have identical physical properties (boiling point, solubility) except that they rotate plane-polarized light in opposite directions. A 50:50 mixture of enantiomers is a racemic mixture and is optically inactive because the rotations cancel.

Stereoisomers that are not mirror images are diastereomers; unlike enantiomers, diastereomers generally have different physical properties.

To name the arrangement at a chiral center, chemists use the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog (CIP) rules. Assign each substituent a priority based on the atomic number of the atom directly attached to the stereocenter (higher atomic number = higher priority). Orient the lowest-priority group away from you, then trace 1 → 2 → 3: clockwise is R (rectus) and counterclockwise is S (sinister).

For alkenes, E/Z notation describes which side the higher-priority groups occupy: E (entgegen, 'opposite') means they are on opposite sides of the double bond, and Z (zusammen, 'together') means they are on the same side. A meso compound has chiral centers but also an internal mirror plane, making the whole molecule achiral.

questions.prompt: A carbon atom is a chiral center (stereocenter) when it is bonded to…
questions.explanation: A stereocenter is a carbon bonded to four different groups, which makes the molecule non-superimposable on its mirror image.

questions.prompt: Enantiomers are best described as…
questions.explanation: Enantiomers are stereoisomers that are non-superimposable mirror images of each other.

questions.prompt: In the Cahn–Ingold–Prelog system, the first (highest) priority is assigned to the substituent with…
questions.explanation: Priority is based on the atomic number of the atom directly attached to the stereocenter — higher atomic number means higher priority (O > N > C > H).

questions.prompt: How are diastereomers different from enantiomers?
options: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are NOT mirror images
questions.explanation: Diastereomers are stereoisomers that are not mirror images of each other, and they generally have different physical properties.

questions.prompt: In alkene E/Z notation, 'E' means the two higher-priority groups are…
options: On the same side of the double bond
On opposite sides of the double bond
Both attached to the same carbon
questions.explanation: E (from the German 'entgegen', meaning opposite) means the higher-priority group on each double-bond carbon is on the opposite side. Z ('zusammen') means the same side.

questions.prompt: How many chiral centers does 2-butanol (CH₃CH(OH)CH₂CH₃) contain?
questions.explanation: Only carbon 2 is bonded to four different groups (–OH, –CH₃, –CH₂CH₃, and –H), so it is the single chiral center.

questions.prompt: A racemic mixture is…
questions.explanation: A racemic mixture is a 50:50 mix of enantiomers. The equal-and-opposite rotations cancel, so it is optically inactive.

questions.prompt: A meso compound is…
options: Achiral despite containing chiral centers (internal mirror plane)
questions.explanation: A meso compound contains chiral centers but also an internal plane of symmetry, which makes the overall molecule achiral and optically inactive.
